terms.meaning: One 'word' of your program: a name, a number, a string, or a symbol such as ; { ( or =.
A name you made up: a variable, function or type name such as count or main.
The compiler has never seen this name declared (created) before this line.
A line that introduces a name and its type, e.g. int count; or int add(int a, int b);
A declaration that actually creates the thing: a function with its { body }, or a variable with storage.
You called a function before telling the compiler it exists, so the compiler had to guess its type.
A function declaration without a body, e.g. int add(int, int); written before main so main can call it.
Something with a memory location that can stand on the LEFT of = (a variable, a[i], *p). x + 1 or 5 are not lvalues.
A temporary value (like 5 or x + 1) that can only appear on the RIGHT of =.
The region of code where a name exists. A variable declared inside { } only exists inside those braces.
The type part of a declaration: int, char, float, struct X, static, const ...
A word that modifies a type, such as const (cannot be changed) or volatile.
The simplest kind of expression: a variable name, a number, a string, or something inside ( ).
A plain name (without :: in front of it), e.g. a variable or function name.
The end of your file. The compiler reached it while still expecting more code (usually a missing } ).
A character the compiler does not recognise as part of C/C++, e.g. a curly quote copied from Word or a PDF.
A literal value written directly in code: 10, 3.14, 'a' or "text".
Letters written right after a number, like the f in 3.5f or the L in 10L. Only a few are allowed.
A backslash code inside a string such as \n (new line) or \t (tab). \\ prints a single backslash.
An explicit conversion from one type to another, written like (float)x or (int)3.7.
A variable that stores a memory address. int *p can hold the address of an int, e.g. p = &x;
Using * on a pointer to reach the value it points to (*p).
The compiler knows a type's name but not what is inside it, usually a struct that was never defined (or is misspelled).
A type that is not a single number or pointer, such as a struct, std::string or std::vector.
Converting to a type that cannot hold every value, e.g. double 3.7 -> int 3 loses the .7.
A version of a function/operator the compiler tried. 'No matching candidate' means none of them accept your arguments.
Several functions with the same name but different parameter lists.
Generic code (like std::vector<T>). Errors 'inside' templates are usually caused by the line in YOUR file shown first.
The official language standard. 'ISO C++ forbids X' means the language rules do not allow X.
A GCC switch that turns some errors into warnings. Do not use it to hide mistakes - fix the code instead.
Still accepted for now, but discouraged and may be removed in future.
A library function the compiler knows about specially (printf, strlen, sqrt...).
The true/false result used by if, while or for.
The program can reach the closing } of the function without executing a return statement.
A function that promises to return a value (its return type is not void).
The program that joins your compiled code with the libraries into one executable. It runs after the compiler.
The linker could not find the body (definition) of a function or variable you used.
The number a program reports when it finishes. 0 means success; anything else means failure.
Argument = the value you pass in a call, add(2, 3). Parameter = the variable that receives it, int add(int a, int b).
The quoted text given to printf/scanf with % placeholders like %d (int), %f (float/double), %c (char), %s (string).
The index inside square brackets, e.g. the i in a[i].
A value an operator works on. In a + b, a and b are the operands of +.
Binary operators take two operands (a + b, a == b); unary operators take one (-x, !x, *p, &x).
A variable or function that belongs to a struct or class, accessed with . or ->.
A named group of names. The C++ standard library lives in namespace std, so cout is really std::cout.
A name created with #define. Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces it with its text (expansion).
A line starting with # (like #include or #define) handled by the preprocessor.
The value given when a variable is created, e.g. the 5 in int x = 5;
An array whose size is a variable, e.g. int a[n]; It cannot be given initial values with = {...}.
One .c/.cpp file after all its #include files have been pasted in.
Words like static, extern, register, auto that say where/how long a variable lives.
A value made of several parts: an array or a struct/class.
Whether an integer type can be negative (int) or not (unsigned int, size_t).
Changing a value from one type to another, e.g. int to double, or a pointer to an integer.
